questions.answer: We need the derivative of an accumulation function with upper limit \(x\). By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt=f(x)\) when \(f\) is continuous. Here \(f(t)=t^2+3\). Therefore the derivative is \(x^2+3\).

We need the derivative of an accumulation function whose upper limit is \(x^2\). Let \(u=x^2\). By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(\frac{d}{du}\int_0^u\cos t\,dt=\cos u\). Then multiply by \(\frac{du}{dx}=2x\). Therefore \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_0^{x^2}\cos t\,dt=2x\cos(x^2)\).

questions.prompt: Compute \(\int_2^5 4x^3\,dx\) using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
questions.answer: We need to evaluate the definite integral using an antiderivative. An antiderivative of \(4x^3\) is \(F(x)=x^4\). By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(\int_2^5 4x^3\,dx=F(5)-F(2)=5^4-2^4=625-16=609\). Therefore the integral equals \(609\).

We need the derivative when the variable is the lower limit. Rewrite \(G(x)=-\int_4^x e^t\,dt\) by reversing the limits. By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_4^x e^t\,dt=e^x\). Therefore \(G'(x)=-e^x\).

We need to differentiate an integral with two variable limits. Use the rule \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_{a(x)}^{b(x)}f(t)\,dt=f(b(x))b'(x)-f(a(x))a'(x)\). Here \(f(t)=1+t^3\), \(b(x)=x^2\), and \(a(x)=x\). Thus \(H'(x)=(1+(x^2)^3)(2x)-(1+x^3)(1)\). Simplifying gives \(H'(x)=2x(1+x^6)-1-x^3\).

We need the derivative of an accumulation function with upper limit \(\sin x\). Let \(u=\sin x\). The Fundamental Theorem gives derivative \(\sqrt{1+u^2}\) with respect to \(u\). The chain rule gives \(\frac{du}{dx}=\cos x\). Therefore the derivative is \(\sqrt{1+\sin^2 x}\cos x\).
We need the derivative of \(F\) at \(x=2\). By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(F'(x)=f(x)\) for a continuous integrand. Therefore \(F'(2)=f(2)=7\).

We need to use the evaluation part of the Fundamental Theorem. An antiderivative is \(F(x)=2x^3-x^2\). Evaluate from \(0\) to \(1\): \(F(1)-F(0)=(2-1)-0=1\). Therefore the definite integral equals \(1\).

questions.prompt: Let \(A(x)=\int_2^x \frac{1}{1+t^2}\,dt\). Find the equation of the tangent line to \(A\) at \(x=2\).
questions.answer: We need the point and slope of \(A\) at \(x=2\). First \(A(2)=\int_2^2\frac{1}{1+t^2}\,dt=0\). By the Fundamental Theorem, \(A'(x)=\frac{1}{1+x^2}\), so \(A'(2)=\frac{1}{5}\). The tangent line at \((2,0)\) is \(y-0=\frac{1}{5}(x-2)\). Therefore the tangent line is \(y=\frac{x-2}{5}\).

We need the derivative with a linear upper limit. Let \(u=3x+1\). By the Fundamental Theorem, the derivative with respect to \(u\) is \(\ln u\). The chain rule gives \(\frac{du}{dx}=3\). Therefore \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_1^{3x+1}\ln t\,dt=3\ln(3x+1)\).
